                                                                                                                             A ﬁnite permutation group G ≤ Sym(Ω) is called 2-closed if G is the largest subgroup
                                                                                                                             of Sym(Ω) which leaves invariant each of the G-orbits for the induced action on Ω × Ω.
                                                                                                                             Introduced by Wielandt in 1969, the concept of 2-closure has developed as one of the
                                                                                                                             most useful approaches for studying relations on a ﬁnite set invariant under a group
                                                                                                                             of permutations of the set; in particular for studying automorphism groups of graphs
                                                                                                                             and digraphs. The concept of total 2-closure switches attention from a particular group
                                                                                                                             action, and is a property intrinsic to the group: a ﬁnite group G is said to be totally
                                                                                                                             2-closed if G is 2-closed in each of its faithful permutation representations. There are
                                                                                                                             inﬁnitely many ﬁnite soluble totally 2-closed groups, and these have been completely
                                                                                                                             characterized, but up to now no insoluble examples were known. It turns out, somewhat
                                                                                                                             surprisingly to us, that there are exactly 6 totally 2-closed ﬁnite nonabelian simple


                                                                                                                         ∗ Corresponding author.

                                                                                                                         under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (CC BY) License which permits use,
                                                                                                                         distribution and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited.

                                                                                                                        groups: the Janko groups J1 , J3 and J4 , together with Ly, Th and the Monster M.
                                                                                                                        Moreover, if a ﬁnite totally 2-closed group has no nontrivial abelian normal subgroup,
                                                                                                                        then we show that it is a direct product of some (but not all) of these simple groups,
                                                                                                                        and there are precisely 47 examples.
                                                                                                                             In the course of obtaining this classiﬁcation, we develop a general framework for
                                                                                                                        studying 2-closures of transitive permutation groups, which we hope will prove useful
                                                                                                                        for investigating representations of ﬁnite groups as automorphism groups of graphs and
                                                                                                                        digraphs, and in particular for attacking the long-standing polycirculant conjecture. In
by 137.205.72.35 on 02/10/26. Re-use and distribution is strictly not permitted, except for Open Access articles.




                                                                                                                        this direction, we apply our results, proving a dual to a 1939 theorem of Frucht from
                                                                                                                        Algebraic Graph Theory. We also pose several open questions concerning closures of
                                                                                                                        permutation groups.

                                                                                                                        Keywords: 2-closed permutation groups; graph representations of groups; simple groups;
                                                                                                                        polycirculant conjecture; Fitting subgroup.

                                                                                                                        Mathematics Subject Classiﬁcation 2020: 20B05, 20E32, 05C20


                                                                                                                    1. Introduction
                                                                                                                    In 1969, Wielandt [39, Deﬁnition 5.3] introduced the concept of 2-closure for a
                                                                                                                    permutation group G on a set Ω. The 2-closure G(2) of G is the set of all g ∈ Sym(Ω)
                                                                                                                    such that g leaves invariant each G-orbit in the induced G-action on ordered pairs
                                                                                                                    from Ω. The 2-closure G(2) is a subgroup of Sym(Ω) containing G [39, Theorem
                                                                                                                    5.4], and G is said to be 2-closed if G(2) = G.
                                                                                                                        It is important to note that the 2-closure of a permutation group G on Ω is not
                                                                                                                    intrinsic to the group G. It can depend on the nature of the action on Ω. For exam-
                                                                                                                    ple, the symmetric group Sym(3) acts faithfully and intransitively on {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
                                                                                                                    with orbits {1, 2, 3} and {4, 5}, and in this action its 2-closure is Sym(3) × C2 ; while
                                                                                                                    Sym(3) is 2-closed in its natural action on {1, 2, 3}. In 2016, Holta suggested a
                                                                                                                    stronger concept independent of the permutation representation. This was adopted
                                                                                                                    and explored by the ﬁrst author with Abdollahi in [1] where it was called total
                                                                                                                    2-closure. To explain the concept we ﬁrst enrich the notation for 2-closure by writ-
                                                                                                                    ing G(2),Ω for the 2-closure of a permutation group G ≤ Sym(Ω). We then deﬁne a
                                                                                                                    group G to be totally 2-closed if G(2),Ω = G whenever G is faithfully represented
                                                                                                                    as a permutation group on Ω. It was proved in [1, Theorem 1] that a ﬁnite totally
                                                                                                                    2-closed group has cyclic center, and moreover [1, Theorem 2] that a ﬁnite nilpotent
                                                                                                                    group is totally 2-closed if and only if it is either cyclic or a direct product of a
                                                                                                                    generalized quaternion group with a cyclic group of odd order.
                                                                                                                        The ﬁrst and fourth authors, with Abdollahi undertook a general study of total
                                                                                                                    2-closure in [2]. They proved [2, Theorem B] that a ﬁnite soluble group is totally
                                                                                                                    2-closed if and only if it is nilpotent, and hence is one of the groups identiﬁed in
                                                                                                                    [1, Theorem 2]. Further they showed in [2, Theorem A] that the Fitting subgroup
                                                                                                                    of a totally 2-closed ﬁnite group is itself totally 2-closed (and hence lies in the
                                                                                                                    family just described). At the time of their writing of the paper [2], no examples
                                                                                                                    of insoluble totally 2-closed groups were known. They studied the structure of an

                                                                                                                    a mathoverﬂow.net/questions/235114/2-closure-of-a-permutation-group.



                                                                                                                                                              2350004-2
                                    March 13, 2024 14:46 WSPC/1664-3607                                                                                      319-BMS           2350004




                                                                                                                                                                                         Totally 2-closed groups


                                                                                                                    insoluble example G of smallest order, showing that G modulo its cyclic center Z(G)
                                                                                                                    has a unique minimal normal subgroup which is nonabelian [2, Proposition 4.1].
                                                                                                                        The ﬁrst purpose of this paper is to seek out ﬁnite insoluble totally 2-closed
                                                                                                                    groups G. We focus on the case where the Fitting subgroup F (G) is trivial, or
                                                                                                                    equivalently, the case where G has no nontrivial abelian normal subgroup. We show
                                                                                                                    ﬁrst that such a group G is a direct product of nonabelian simple groups, each of
                                                                                                                    which is itself totally 2-closed (see Theorem 2.5). In light of this result, we decided
by 137.205.72.35 on 02/10/26. Re-use and distribution is strictly not permitted, except for Open Access articles.




                                                                                                                    that our next challenge should be to ﬁnd all totally 2-closed ﬁnite simple groups.
                                                                                                                    The 2-closure condition seemed so strong that we initially believed that we would
                                                                                                                    ﬁnd no examples. Surprisingly (to us) such groups do indeed exist, but they are
                                                                                                                    rare, and the only examples are six of the sporadic simple groups.
                   Bull. Math. Sci. 2024.14. Downloaded from www.worldscientific.com




                                                                                                                    Theorem 1.1. Let T be a nonabelian ﬁnite simple group. Then T is totally 2-closed
                                                                                                                    if and only if T is one of the groups J1 , J3 , J4 , Ly, Th or M.
                                                                                                                        Theorem 1.1 gives us the building blocks of ﬁnite totally 2-closed groups with
                                                                                                                    trivial Fitting subgroup. We were able to use this result as the basis of an inductive
                                                                                                                    approach yielding the following complete classiﬁcation of all such groups.

                                                                                                                    Theorem 1.2. Let G be a nontrivial ﬁnite group with trivial Fitting subgroup.
                                                                                                                    Then G is totally 2-closed if and only if each of the following holds:
                                                                                                                    (1) G = T1 × · · · × Tr , where the Ti are nonabelian ﬁnite simple groups and r ≤ 5;
                                                                                                                    (2) Ti ∼
                                                                                                                            Tj for each i = j; and
                                                                                                                            =
                                                                                                                    (3) One of the following holds:
                                                                                                                         (i) Ti ∈ {J1 , J3 , J4 , Th, Ly} for each i ≤ r; or
                                                                                                                        (ii) Ti ∈ {J1 , J3 , J4 , Ly, M} for each i ≤ r.

                                                                                                                    Corollary 1.3. There are precisely 47 ﬁnite totally 2-closed groups with trivial
                                                                                                                    Fitting subgroup.
                                                                                                                        Proving these results involved a wide variety of methods, and we needed to
                                                                                                                    develop several tools which we hope will assist future analyses of ﬁnite totally 2-
                                                                                                                    closed groups.
                                                                                                                        The second purpose of the paper is to develop general machinery to study 2-
                                                                                                                    closures of transitive permutation groups. This is not only crucial for our proof of
                                                                                                                    Theorem 1.2, but is also key in order to make further progress on the polycirculant
                                                                                                                    conjecture (see Sec. 1.1 for more details).

                                                                                                                    1.1. Motivation from graph theory and the polycirculant conjecture
                                                                                                                    The concept of 2-closure is a very combinatorial notion, and there is indeed a
                                                                                                                    close relationship between 2-closed permutation groups and digraphs: each subset
                                                                                                                    A ⊆ Ω × Ω may be viewed as the arc-set of a digraph Γ = (Ω, A) with vertex-set Ω
                                                                                                                    and with a directed edge (an arc) from α to β for each (α, β) ∈ A. The automor-
                                                                                                                    phism group Aut(Γ) of Γ is deﬁned as the subgroup of all permutations of Ω which

                                                                                                                                                             2350004-3
                                    March 13, 2024 14:46 WSPC/1664-3607                                                                                   319-BMS       2350004




                                                                                                                    M. Arezoomand et al.


                                                                                                                    leave the arc-set A invariant. In particular, each element of (Aut(Γ))(2),Ω leaves A
                                                                                                                    invariant and hence is an automorphism of Γ. Thus (Aut(Γ))(2),Ω ⊆ Aut(Γ), and
                                                                                                                    the reverse inclusion holds by the deﬁnition of 2-closure. Therefore (Aut(Γ))(2),Ω =
                                                                                                                    Aut(Γ). The same argument also shows that (Aut(Γ))(2),Ω = Aut(Γ) when Γ is an
                                                                                                                    undirected graph. Thus, to summarize, for each (di)graph Γ with vertex set Ω, the
                                                                                                                    automorphism group Aut(Γ) is a 2-closed subgroup of Sym(Ω). In fact, for each
                                                                                                                    permutation group G ≤ Sym(Ω), the 2-closure G(2),Ω is equal to the intersection of
by 137.205.72.35 on 02/10/26. Re-use and distribution is strictly not permitted, except for Open Access articles.




                                                                                                                    the groups Aut(Γ) over all digraphs Γ = (Ω, A) for which the arc-set A is a G-orbit
                                                                                                                    in Ω × Ω.
                                                                                                                        In particular, if G ≤ Sym(Ω) is transitive on Ω and if A is a G-orbit in Ω × Ω
                                                                                                                    not equal to the diagonal {(α, α) | α ∈ Ω}, then the digraph Γ = (Ω, A) is called
                                                                                                                    a G-orbital digraph. The study of G-orbital digraphs goes back to the work of
                   Bull. Math. Sci. 2024.14. Downloaded from www.worldscientific.com




                                                                                                                    Higman [17] at approximately the same time as Wielandt’s work on closures in the
                                                                                                                    late 1960s.
                                                                                                                        Let Γ = (Ω, A) be a digraph as above, with vertex-set Ω and arc-set A ⊆ Ω × Ω.
                                                                                                                    An element of Sym(Ω) in which all cycles have the same length is called semiregular ;
                                                                                                                    while an automorphism α of Γ is called semiregular if the permutation induced by
                                                                                                                    α on the vertices of Γ is semiregular. The graph Γ is said to be polycirculant if
                                                                                                                    Aut(Γ) contains a nontrivial semiregular element.
                                                                                                                        In 1981 [29], Marus̆ic̆ made the following well-known conjecture: Every ﬁnite
                                                                                                                    connected vertex-transitive digraph is a polycirculant. This is known in the lit-
                                                                                                                    erature as the polycirculant conjecture, and was also made (independently) by
                                                                                                                    Jordan in 1988 [21]. The conjecture was generalized to the following by Klin at the
                                                                                                                    British Combinatorial Conference in 1995: Every ﬁnite transitive 2-closed permu-
                                                                                                                    tation group of degree greater than 1 contains a semiregular element. As explained
                                                                                                                    above, the automorphism group of every ﬁnite digraph Γ with vertex set Ω is a
                                                                                                                    2-closed subgroup of Sym(Ω). Thus, Klin’s generalization is stronger than the poly-
                                                                                                                    circulant conjecture. We point the reader to the beautiful survey [24] by Kutnar
                                                                                                                    and Marus̆ic̆ for further observations on the underlying philosophy behind the con-
                                                                                                                    jecture, and its importance in graph theory. See also [8, Sec. 1.3.4] and the more
                                                                                                                    recent survey [3].
                                                                                                                        There have been two main approaches to proving the polycirculant conjecture
                                                                                                                    (or rather, Klin’s generalized conjecture). The ﬁrst has been to study those transi-
                                                                                                                    tive permutation groups which do not contain a semiregular element (such groups
                                                                                                                    are called elusive), and show that no such group can be 2-closed. This approach has
                                                                                                                    led to some outstanding breakthroughs, one of the most signiﬁcant of which was
                                                                                                                    Giudici’s theorem [15]. There, it is proved that apart from a family of groups of prod-
                                                                                                                    uct action type associated to the Mathieu group M11 , all quasiprimitive permutation
                                                                                                                    groups contain semiregular elements (a permutation group is called quasiprimitive
                                                                                                                    if every nontrivial normal subgroup is transitive). Further, of those quasiprimitive
                                                                                                                    groups which fail to have semiregular elements, none are 2-closed. This, combined
                                                                                                                    with [10, Theorem 5.5], yields the proof of the polycirculant conjecture in the case
                                                                                                                    where the automorphism group of the digraph in question is almost simple.

                                                                                                                                                           2350004-4
                                    March 13, 2024 14:46 WSPC/1664-3607                                                                                      319-BMS        2350004




                                                                                                                                                                                      Totally 2-closed groups


                                                                                                                        The second main approach is the dual to the ﬁrst approach: to study the 2-closed
                                                                                                                    transitive permutation groups, and prove that all such groups contain semiregular
                                                                                                                    elements. The ﬁrst step in such an approach is to develop machinery to determine
                                                                                                                    the 2-closure of a given transitive permutation group. When the given transitive
                                                                                                                    group is primitive, a powerful theorem of Liebeck et al. [26] shows that, apart
                                                                                                                    from a ﬁnite list of exceptions and two known inﬁnite families, the 2-closure of
                                                                                                                    an almost simple simply primitive group G ≤ Sym(Ω) is also almost simple, with
by 137.205.72.35 on 02/10/26. Re-use and distribution is strictly not permitted, except for Open Access articles.




                                                                                                                    the same socle as G. Further progress on the primitive case was made by Praeger
                                                                                                                    and Saxl in [31], where it is shown that if G is an arbitrary primitive group, then
                                                                                                                    soc(G) = G(2),Ω , apart from some known families of exceptions.
                                                                                                                        These results greatly facilitate the computation of the 2-closure of a primitive
                                                                                                                    permutation group. On the other hand, there has been little to no progress in
                   Bull. Math. Sci. 2024.14. Downloaded from www.worldscientific.com




                                                                                                                    building general techniques to determining the 2-closure of an imprimitive group.
                                                                                                                    Since Giudici’s theorem proves the polycirculant conjecture in the primitive case,
                                                                                                                    building such techniques is key for further progress.
                                                                                                                        With this in mind, part of the motivation for this paper was to study 2-closures
                                                                                                                    of imprimitive permutation groups which induce a faithful 2-closed action on a set
                                                                                                                    of maximal blocks. Our main results are Theorems 3.8 and 3.10 (for notational
                                                                                                                    convenience, we postpone their statements until Sec. 3).


                                                                                                                    1.2. An application: Frucht representations
                                                                                                                    Before describing our approach to proving Theorems 1.1 and 1.2, we would like
                                                                                                                    to draw attention to a graph theoretic consequence of our results, which may be
                                                                                                                    of independent interest. In 1939, Frucht [14] conﬁrmed a conjecture of König that
                                                                                                                    every ﬁnite group G can be written as the automorphism group of a ﬁnite simple
                                                                                                                    undirected graph Γ. We will say that a faithful permutation representation G →
                                                                                                                    GΩ ≤ Sym(Ω) of G on a ﬁnite set Ω is a Frucht representation of G if there exists
                                                                                                                    a set E of unordered pairs from Ω such that GΩ is the automorphism group of the
                                                                                                                    ﬁnite simple undirected graph Γ = Γ(Ω, E). Since Aut(Γ) is 2-closed, Theorem 1.2
                                                                                                                    implies the following, which can be viewed as a dual to Frucht’s theorem in the case
                                                                                                                    where F (G) = 1.

                                                                                                                    Corollary 1.4. Let G be a nontrivial ﬁnite group with trivial Fitting subgroup, and
                                                                                                                    assume that every faithful permutation representation of G is a Frucht represen-
                                                                                                                    tation. Then G = T1 × · · · × Tr , where the Ti are pairwise non-isomorphic ﬁnite
                                                                                                                    simple groups; r ≤ 5; and either

                                                                                                                     (i) for each i ≤ r, Ti ∈ {J1 , J3 , J4 , Th, Ly}; or
                                                                                                                    (ii) for each i ≤ r, Ti ∈ {J1 , J3 , J4 , Ly, M}.

                                                                                                                       It is an open question as to whether the converse of Corollary 1.4 holds. This,
                                                                                                                    and further open questions concerning closures of permutation groups are posed
                                                                                                                    below.

                                                                                                                                                              2350004-5
                                    March 13, 2024 14:46 WSPC/1664-3607                                                                                   319-BMS       2350004




                                                                                                                    M. Arezoomand et al.


                                                                                                                    1.3. Some open questions
                                                                                                                    We mention a few open questions about closures of permutation groups. Firstly,
                                                                                                                    since we have considered only groups with trivial Fitting subgroup in this paper,
                                                                                                                    we ask.

                                                                                                                    Question 1. Are there any ﬁnite insoluble totally 2-closed groups with nontrivial
                                                                                                                    Fitting subgroup? If so, can we classify them?
by 137.205.72.35 on 02/10/26. Re-use and distribution is strictly not permitted, except for Open Access articles.




                                                                                                                        One of the ultimate goals of this programme of work is to classify all ﬁnite
                                                                                                                    totally 2-closed groups. Given the results in this paper, this goal would be realized
                                                                                                                    with a complete answer to Question 1. See Sec. 8 for some remarks on the obstacles
                                                                                                                    involved in answering this question.
                   Bull. Math. Sci. 2024.14. Downloaded from www.worldscientific.com




                                                                                                                        The analogous concept of total k-closure may be deﬁned for arbitrary positive
                                                                                                                    integers k, namely, G is totally k-closed if, for every faithful representation G ≤
                                                                                                                    Sym(Ω), G is equal to the set of all elements g ∈ Sym(Ω) such that g leaves invariant
                                                                                                                    each G-orbit in the induced G-action on ordered k-tuples from Ω. This concept has
                                                                                                                    been explored by Churikov and the third author in [11]. For each k ≥ 2, it follows
                                                                                                                    from [39, Theorem 5.8] that, if G is totally (k − 1)-closed then G is also totally
                                                                                                                    k-closed. On the other hand, by [11, Theorem 1.2], there are inﬁnitely many ﬁnite
                                                                                                                    totally k-closed groups which are not totally (k − 1)-closed, and this is true even for
                                                                                                                    abelian p-groups for each prime p. The paper [11] gives a discussion of the topic and
                                                                                                                    poses three open problems about total k-closure (where k ≥ 3) for ﬁnite nilpotent
                                                                                                                    groups, soluble groups, and sporadic simple groups — all problems which have been
                                                                                                                    resolved for k = 2, in [1, 2] and this paper. It follows from [39, Theorem 5.11] that
                                                                                                                    an alternating group An (with n ≥ 5) is not totally k-closed for any k ≤ n − 2, so
                                                                                                                    we further ask.

                                                                                                                    Question 2. Are there any ﬁnite simple groups of Lie type which are totally
                                                                                                                    3-closed? If so, ﬁnd them all.
                                                                                                                       The example of the alternating groups above shows that there is no ﬁxed integer
                                                                                                                    k such that all nonabelian ﬁnite simple groups are totally k-closed. It is worthwhile
                                                                                                                    to note, however, that for any faithful representation of a ﬁnite nonabelian simple
                                                                                                                    group G, there is a G-orbit on which G acts non-trivially and hence faithfully;
                                                                                                                    applying [39, Theorem 5.12] to the G-action on this orbit we deduce that G is
                                                                                                                    totally n-closed, where n = |G|. Since the alternating groups seem like exceptional
                                                                                                                    cases in practice, we therefore ask.

                                                                                                                    Question 3. Is there a ﬁxed integer k such that all nonabelian ﬁnite simple groups
                                                                                                                    which are not alternating groups are totally k-closed?
                                                                                                                        We remark that we submitted Questions 1–3 to the latest (20th) edition of the
                                                                                                                    Kourovka notebook (a collection of unsolved problems in Group Theory) which has
                                                                                                                    just been released [23]. They appear as Questions 20.1–20.3 — the ﬁrst three of 126
                                                                                                                    new open problems.

                                                                                                                                                           2350004-6
                                    March 13, 2024 14:46 WSPC/1664-3607                                                                                       319-BMS       2350004




                                                                                                                                                                                       Totally 2-closed groups


                                                                                                                       Finally, and as mentioned above, it is not clear whether or not the converse to
                                                                                                                    Corollary 1.4 holds. So we ask.
                                                                                                                    Question 4. Let G = T1 × · · ·× Tr , where the Ti are pairwise non-isomorphic ﬁnite
                                                                                                                    simple groups; r ≤ 5; and either
                                                                                                                     (i) for each i ≤ r, Ti ∈ {J1 , J3 , J4 , Th, Ly}; or
                                                                                                                    (ii) for each i ≤ r, Ti ∈ {J1 , J3 , J4 , Ly, M}.
by 137.205.72.35 on 02/10/26. Re-use and distribution is strictly not permitted, except for Open Access articles.




                                                                                                                    Then is it true that every faithful permutation representation of G is a Frucht
                                                                                                                    representation? If not, then which (if any) of the listed 47 groups does have this
                                                                                                                    property?
                   Bull. Math. Sci. 2024.14. Downloaded from www.worldscientific.com




                                                                                                                    1.4. Structure of the paper
                                                                                                                    In the remained of this section, we outline our approach to the proofs of Theo-
                                                                                                                    rems 1.1 and 1.2, and detail the structure of the paper. The fundamental starting
                                                                                                                    point is Wielandt’s Dissection Theorem [39, Dissection Theorem 6.5] which for
                                                                                                                    convenience we state as Theorem 2.1. It is an invaluable tool, and in particular it
                                                                                                                    underpins our proof of Theorem 2.5, which we present in Sec. 2.
                                                                                                                        As mentioned above, Theorem 2.5 reduces our classiﬁcation of ﬁnite totally 2-
                                                                                                                    closed groups G with trivial Fitting subgroup to the case where G is a direct product
                                                                                                                    of nonabelian simple groups, which are ‘independent’ of each other in the sense that
                                                                                                                    each of the simple direct factors is not isomorphic to a section of the direct product
                                                                                                                    of the others. (We comment on this condition in relation to the sporadic simple
                                                                                                                    groups in Remark 2.6). Our next step is to reduce further: in Proposition 2.10, we
                                                                                                                    show that such a group G is totally 2-closed if and only if no simple direct factor
                                                                                                                    of G admits a nontrivial factorization, and each (not necessarily faithful) transitive
                                                                                                                    permutation representation of G is 2-closed.
                                                                                                                        This suggests two natural avenues to pursue. The ﬁrst is to use the classiﬁcation
                                                                                                                    of the maximal factorizations of the nonabelian simple groups in [27] to eliminate
                                                                                                                    many families of simple groups from being direct factors of G. We do this in Sec. 2.3,
                                                                                                                    where we show, in particular, that the simple direct factors of G are either sporadic
                                                                                                                    groups or exceptional groups of Lie type.
                                                                                                                        Our second natural avenue to pursue concerns transitive actions of such groups
                                                                                                                    G. Strong restrictions on the 2-closures of primitive almost simple groups were
                                                                                                                    obtained in [26]. With these restrictions in mind for the case where G is simple,
                                                                                                                    we develop powerful reduction theorems in Sec. 3 for general transitive imprimitive
                                                                                                                    permutation groups G which induce a faithful 2-closed action on a set of nontrivial
                                                                                                                    blocks of imprimitivity: we show that either G itself is 2-closed, or the 2-closure of G
                                                                                                                    has a very particular structure. This provides further criteria to determine whether
                                                                                                                    or not such permutation groups are 2-closed (see, in particular, Theorem 3.10).
                                                                                                                        The tools developed in Secs. 2 and 3 are suﬃcient to begin our analysis of the
                                                                                                                    2-closures of permutation representations of the ﬁnite simple groups. In Secs. 4 and
                                                                                                                    6, we deal with the sporadic groups other than J4 , and the exceptional groups of Lie

                                                                                                                                                              2350004-7
                                    March 13, 2024 14:46 WSPC/1664-3607                                                                                   319-BMS        2350004




                                                                                                                    M. Arezoomand et al.


                                                                                                                    type, respectively. The case of G = J4 is delicate, and requires a nuanced approach,
                                                                                                                    see Sec. 5. These three sections complete the proof of Theorem 1.1.
                                                                                                                        Section 7 is reserved for the study of 2-closures of direct products of ﬁnite simple
                                                                                                                    groups, and the proof of Theorem 1.2.
                                                                                                                        Finally, in Sec. 8, we make some concluding remarks on the question of classi-
                                                                                                                    fying the ﬁnite insoluble totally 2-closed groups with nontrivial Fitting subgroup.
                                                                                                                    We also prove a useful reduction theorem for this problem.
by 137.205.72.35 on 02/10/26. Re-use and distribution is strictly not permitted, except for Open Access articles.




                                                                                                                    Notation: Most of our notation is standard. For a ﬁnite group G, we write Z(G),
                                                                                                                    F (G), Φ(G) and [G, G] for the center, Fitting subgroup, Frattini subgroup, and
                                                                                                                    derived subgroup of G, respectively.
                                                                                                                        For a set Ω, we write Sym(Ω) and Alt(Ω) for the symmetric and alternating
                   Bull. Math. Sci. 2024.14. Downloaded from www.worldscientific.com




                                                                                                                    group on Ω, respectively. If a ﬁnite group G acts on Ω, we write GΩ for the image
                                                                                                                    of the induced action of G on Ω.
                                                                                                                        For group names, we use conventions from the Atlas [12, especially p. xx], except
                                                                                                                    that we write Alt(n) and Sym(n) for the alternating and symmetric groups of
                                                                                                                    degree n.


                                                                                                                    2. Applying Wielandt’s Dissection Theorem
                                                                                                                    As we mentioned in Sec. 1, Wielandt’s Dissection Theorem [39, Dissection Theorem
                                                                                                                    6.5] is a fundamental tool for studying 2-closure. For convenience we state it here.
                                                                                                                    Note that, for G ≤ Sym(Ω) and δ ∈ Ω, we denote by Gδ the stabilizer of δ in G,
                                                                                                                    and by δ G the G-orbit in Ω containing δ. Also if Γ ⊆ Ω and Γ is G-invariant, then
                                                                                                                    GΓ denotes the permutation group on Γ induced by G.

                                                                                                                    Theorem 2.1 (Wielandt’s Dissection Theorem). Let G ≤ Sym(Ω), and sup-
                                                                                                                    pose that Ω is the disjoint union Ω = Γ∪Δ such that both Γ and Δ are G-invariant.
                                                                                                                    Then the following are equivalent :

                                                                                                                    (a) GΓ × GΔ ≤ G(2),Ω ;
                                                                                                                    (b) G = Gγ Gδ for all γ ∈ Γ, δ ∈ Δ;
                                                                                                                    (c) Gδ is transitive on γ G for all γ ∈ Γ, δ ∈ Δ.

                                                                                                                       In this section, we discuss some ways in which this result can be applied. To
                                                                                                                    begin, we state the following helpful application given in [2]. Here, for a sub-
                                                                                                                    group H of a group G, we denote by CoreG (H) the core of H in G, that is,
                                                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                    CoreG (H) = g∈G H g , the largest normal subgroup of G contained in H. By a
                                                                                                                    nontrivial factorization of G we mean a factorization G = HK with both H and
                                                                                                                    K proper subgroups of G.

                                                                                                                    Lemma 2.2 ([2, Lemma 3.1]). Let G be a ﬁnite totally 2-closed group such that
                                                                                                                    G admits a nontrivial factorization G = HK with

                                                                                                                                                CoreG (H) ∩ CoreG (K) = 1.

                                                                                                                                                           2350004-8
                                    March 13, 2024 14:46 WSPC/1664-3607                                                                                      319-BMS          2350004




                                                                                                                                                                                             Totally 2-closed groups


                                                                                                                    Then G = CoreG (H) × CoreG (K) and both CoreG (H) and CoreG (K) are totally
                                                                                                                    2-closed. In particular, if H ∩ K = 1, then G = H × K and both H and K are
                                                                                                                    totally 2-closed.
                                                                                                                       Lemma 2.2 has the following important consequence for simple groups.

                                                                                                                    Corollary 2.3. Let T be a ﬁnite nonabelian simple group. If T is totally 2-closed,
                                                                                                                    then T admits no nontrivial factorization.
by 137.205.72.35 on 02/10/26. Re-use and distribution is strictly not permitted, except for Open Access articles.




                                                                                                                    Proof. Suppose that T is totally 2-closed. If T = HK is a nontrivial factorization,
                                                                                                                    then the cores CoreT (H) = CoreT (K) = 1 since T is simple, and this contradicts
                                                                                                                    Lemma 2.2. Hence T has no nontrivial factorizations.
                   Bull. Math. Sci. 2024.14. Downloaded from www.worldscientific.com




                                                                                                                       The following result from Wielandt [39] is also useful when making a detailed
                                                                                                                    analysis of 2-closures.
                                                                                                                    Theorem 2.4 ([39, Theorem 5.6]). Let G ≤ Sym(Ω) and x ∈ Sym(Ω). Then
                                                                                                                    x ∈ G(2),Ω if and only if, for all α, β ∈ Ω, there exists g ∈ G such that αx = αg and
                                                                                                                    βx = βg .


                                                                                                                    2.1. Reduction to direct products of nonabelian finite simple
                                                                                                                         groups
                                                                                                                    In this section, we reduce our proof of Theorem 1.2 to particular direct products of
                                                                                                                    ﬁnite simple groups. Before we state our main result, we remind the reader of some
                                                                                                                    standard terminology: a nontrivial group X is said to be a section of a group G if
                                                                                                                    there are subgroups L  H ≤ G such that H/L ∼    = X. Our reduction theorem can
                                                                                                                    now be stated as follows.

                                                                                                                    Theorem 2.5. Let G be a nontrivial ﬁnite totally 2-closed group such that F (G) =
                                                                                                                    1. Then G = T1 × · · · × Tr for some r ≥ 1, where for each i ≤ r, Ti is a ﬁnite
                                                                                                                                                                                                 
                                                                                                                    nonabelian simple group which is totally 2-closed, and Ti is not a section of j=i Tj .

                                                                                                                    Proof. Since G is ﬁnite, nontrivial, and F (G) = 1, a minimal normal subgroup M
                                                                                                                    of G is a direct product of nonabelian ﬁnite simple groups. If M = G then, as M
                                                                                                                    is minimal normal, the group G would itself be a nonabelian simple group which is
                                                                                                                    totally 2-closed, and the conclusion holds with r = 1. Thus, we may assume that
                                                                                                                    M = G, and M = S1 × · · · × Ss with each Si a ﬁnite nonabelian simple group. We
                                                                                                                    note that the minimal normal subgroups of M are precisely the subgroups
                                                                                                                                 Si = {(x1 , . . . , xs ) | xj = 1 for j = i, and xi ∈ Si } ∼
                                                                                                                                                                                              = Si ,
                                                                                                                    for i = 1, . . . , s (see, for example [32, Theorem 4.16(iv)]). By the ‘Odd Order The-
                                                                                                                    orem’, since each of the Si is a ﬁnite nonabelian simple group, each Si has a non-
                                                                                                                    trivial Sylow 2-subgroup, Pi say, and hence P = P1 × · · · × Ps is a (nontrivial)
                                                                                                                    Sylow 2-subgroup of M . By the Frattini argument (see, for example [34, 5.2.14]),

                                                                                                                                                              2350004-9
                                    March 13, 2024 14:46 WSPC/1664-3607                                                                                    319-BMS        2350004




                                                                                                                    M. Arezoomand et al.


                                                                                                                    G = NG (P )M . Now, NM (P ) = NS1 (P1 ) × · · · × NSs (Ps ), and NM (P ) projects to a
                                                                                                                    proper subgroup N  (Pi ) of Si , for each i. In particular M ≤ NG (P ). Hence the core
                                                                                                                                           Si
                                                                                                                    X = CoreG (NG (P )) does not contain M , and so X ∩ M = 1 since M is a minimal
                                                                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                    normal subgroup of G. Also since M is normal in G, CoreG (M ) = g∈G M g = M .
                                                                                                                    Then, since G is totally 2-closed, it follows from Lemma 2.2 that G = X × M and
                                                                                                                    both X and M are totally 2-closed. Since M = G it follows that X = 1 and since M
                                                                                                                    is a minimal normal subgroup of G we conclude that M = S1 is a ﬁnite nonabelian
by 137.205.72.35 on 02/10/26. Re-use and distribution is strictly not permitted, except for Open Access articles.




                                                                                                                    simple group.
                                                                                                                        Thus each minimal normal subgroup of G is a totally 2-closed, ﬁnite nonabelian
                                                                                                                    simple group and is a direct factor of G. Applying this argument recursively we
                                                                                                                    conclude that G = T1 × T2 × · · · × Tr for some r ≥ 2, where each Ti is a totally
                                                                                                                    2-closed, ﬁnite nonabelian simple group. For 1 ≤ j ≤ r let πj denote the projection
                   Bull. Math. Sci. 2024.14. Downloaded from www.worldscientific.com




                                                                                                                    πj : G → Tj given by (t1 , . . . , tr ) → tj , and let Tj denote the minimal normal
                                                                                                                    subgroup of G deﬁned similarly to the Si above.
                                                                                                                        Let i, j be distinct integers between 1 and r. We show next that Ti is not a
                                                                                                                    section of Tj . Suppose that this is false, so there exist subgroups L  H ≤ Tj
                                                                                                                    such that H/L ∼  = Ti , or equivalently, there exists an epimorphism ϕ : H → Ti
                                                                                                                    with kernel L. Without loss of generality, assume that i = 1 and j = 2, and let
                                                                                                                    J = {(ϕ(h), h, 1, . . . , 1) | h ∈ H} and K = 1×T2 ×· · ·×Tr . Clearly both J and K are
                                                                                                                    proper subgroups of G. Moreover, since ϕ is an epimorphism it follows that G = JK
                                                                                                                    is a nontrivial factorization, and since K is normal in G we have CoreG (K) =
                                                                                                                    K. We claim that CoreG (J) = 1. Now, CoreG (J) ≤ J < T1 × T2 × 1 · · · × 1,
                                                                                                                    and if CoreG (J) = 1 then CoreG (J) would contain at least one of the minimal
                                                                                                                    normal subgroups of G, namely one of T1 , . . . , Tr , so CoreG (J) would contain T1
                                                                                                                    or T2 . Let x = (ϕ(h), h, 1, . . . , 1) ∈ CoreG (J). If x1 = ϕ(h) = 1 then h = 1, so
                                                                                                                    CoreG (J) ∩ T1 = 1. Also if x ∈ T2 , then x1 = ϕ(h) = 1 so h ∈ Ker(ϕ) = L. Since
                                                                                                                    L is a proper subgroup of T2 it follows that CoreG (J) does not contain T2 either.
                                                                                                                    Hence CoreG (J) = 1 as claimed. It now follows from Lemma 2.2 that G = 1 × K,
                                                                                                                    which is a contradiction. Thus none of the Ti is a section of any of the other Tj
                                                                                                                    (and in particular the Ti are pairwise non-isomorphic).
                                                                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                       Finally, suppose that, for some i ≤ r, Ti is a section of K := j=i Tj . Then
                                                                                                                    there are subgroups L  H ≤ K such that H/L ∼      = Ti . Let H, L be subgroups of K
                                                                                                                    with this property such that |H| is as small as possible. Identify K with the normal
                                                                                                                                                                                               
                                                                                                                    subgroup j=i Tj of G. Let 1 ≤ j ≤ r with j = i, and consider Hj := H ∩( k=j Tk ),
                                                                                                                    the kernel of the restriction πj |H to H of the projection πj . We will identify πj (H)
                                                                                                                    with the quotient H/Hj so that, for each subgroup J ≤ H, the image πj (J) is
                                                                                                                    identiﬁed with JHj /Hj . In particular πj (L) = LHj /Hj . Then
                                                                                                                        Q := πj (H)/πj (L) = (H/Hj )/(LHj /Hj ) ∼
                                                                                                                                                                = H/(LHj ) ∼
                                                                                                                                                                           = (H/L)/(LHj /L),
                                                                                                                    a quotient of the simple group H/L ∼= Ti . Thus Q ∼= Ti or 1. Now, πj (L)  πj (H) ≤
                                                                                                                    Tj , and by the previous paragraph Ti is not a section of Tj , and hence the quotient
                                                                                                                    πj (H)/πj (L) ∼
                                                                                                                                   Ti . Thus, Q must be trivial, and hence H = LHj . This, however,
                                                                                                                                   =
                                                                                                                    implies that Ti ∼= H/L = (LHj )/L ∼ = Hj /(L ∩ Hj ), and so, by the minimality of

                                                                                                                    |H|, we conclude that H = Hj , that is to say, πj (H) = 1. Since this holds for each
                                                                                                                                          
