                                                                                                                        construct the new set S+1 .
                                                                                                                        (a) If, T [T :H] has base size 2, then it follows from Theorem 3.10(3) that, for
                                                                                                                            each K < H, we have T [T :K] = T (2),[T :K] . Thus proper subgroups of H
                                                                                                                            need no further testing.
                                                                                                                        (b) We remove from S each H ∈ S with T (H) = and, in addition, if T [T :H]
by 137.205.72.35 on 02/10/26. Re-use and distribution is strictly not permitted, except for Open Access articles.




                                                                                                                            has base size 2, we also remove all proper subgroups of H. Let S+1 denote
                                                                                                                            the resulting set of subgroups.
                                                                                                                        (c) If S+1 = ∅ then we have successfully shown that T [T :H] = T (2),[T :H] for
                                                                                                                            every proper subgroup H of T , we conclude that T is totally 2-closed, and
                                                                                                                            the analysis is completed.
                                                                                                                        (d) On the other hand if S+1 = ∅, then by its construction it is not diﬃcult
                   Bull. Math. Sci. 2024.14. Downloaded from www.worldscientific.com




                                                                                                                            to check that S+1 has property (∗) with + 1 in place of .

                                                                                                                       We begin by applying this strategy to the group HN, and here we do not need
                                                                                                                    to proceed past stage (1) of Step 1 in Strategy 4.5.

                                                                                                                    Proposition 4.6. The Harada Norton group HN is not totally 2-closed.

                                                                                                                    Proof. Let T = HN, the Harada Norton group. One of the groups H ∈ S1 in Strat-
                                                                                                                    egy 4.5 is H = 4.HS, and Aut(T ) = T.2 has a primitive permutation representation
                                                                                                                    on a set of size 1,539,000, with point stabilizer H.2. For the normal subgroup T ,
                                                                                                                    this representation is permutationally isomorphic to its transitive action on [T : H],
                                                                                                                    which has rank 9, with all subdegrees distinct, see [19, Lemma 2.18.1]. Thus, in par-
                                                                                                                    ticular, H.2 must leave invariant each H-orbit in [T : H]. Hence Aut(T ) also has
                                                                                                                    rank 9 on [T : H]. We conclude that T (2),[T :H] contains T.2, so T is not totally
                                                                                                                    2-closed.

                                                                                                                        We now move on to the group J1 , where we must use both stages of Steps 1 and
                                                                                                                    2 of Strategy 4.5.

                                                                                                                    Remark 4.7. At various stages in the remainder of the paper, we will us the
                                                                                                                    following fact: if K is a proper nontrivial subgroup of a group T and K is contained
                                                                                                                    in a core-free subgroup H of T such that T [T :H] has base size 2, then also T [T :K]
                                                                                                                    has base size 2. (This follows from the fact that T [T :H] having a base of size 2 means
                                                                                                                    that, for some g ∈ T , H ∩ H g acts trivially on [T : H] and hence H ∩ H g = 1 since
                                                                                                                    H is core-free in T , whence also its subgroup K ∩ K g is trivial.)

                                                                                                                    Proposition 4.11. The monster M is totally 2-closed.

                                                                                                                    Proof. Let T = M. As usual our task, using Strategy 4.5, is to prove that T Ω =
                                                                                                                    T (2),Ω , where Ω = [T : H], for each proper nontrivial subgroup H of T . Since T =
                                                                                                                    Aut(T ) and T has no 2-transitive representations, it follows from Lemma 4.3(b)(i)
                                                                                                                    that this holds for all maximal subgroups H. Thus we proceed to stage (2) of Step
                                                                                                                    1 in Strategy 4.5, and here, by Proposition 4.10, the only maximal subgroup M
                                                                                                                    such that T [T :M] has base size at least 3 is M = 2.B. Hence the set S2 formed in
                                                                                                                    Step 1 consists, up to conjugacy, of all proper nontrivial subgroups of M .

                                                                                                                    Proposition 4.12. The O’Nan group ON is not totally 2-closed.

                                                                                                                    Proof. Let T = ON and let M be a maximal subgroup of T with M = L3 (7) : 2.
                                                                                                                    Also let H = M  (the derived subgroup), so |M : H| = 2. By Corollary 4.4,
                                                                                                                    T [T :M] = T (2),[T :M] . We check, using GAP [35], that no two-point stabilizer in
                                                                                                                    M [T :M] is contained in H. Hence, (M ∩ M t )H = M for all t ∈ T , that is to say,
                                                                                                                    condition (ii) of Theorem 3.10(1) holds. Since T [T :M] = T (2),[T :M] , Theorem 3.10(1)
                                                                                                                    applies, and we conclude that T [T :H] is not 2-closed. Thus, T is not totally 2-closed.

                                                                                                                       Now, we deal with the Conway and Fischer groups Co2 and Fi23 , and then the
                                                                                                                    baby monster B.

                                                                                                                    Proposition 4.14. Neither the second Conway group Co2 nor the Fischer group
                                                                                                                    Fi23 is totally 2-closed.

                                                                                                                    Proof. Let T ∈ {Co2 , Fi23 }. Consider the following maximal subgroup M of T ,
                                                                                                                    namely, M = U6 (2) : 2 if T = Co2 , and M = O8+ (3) : Sym(3) if T = Fi23 . In each
                                                                                                                    case, T [T :M] has rank 3. Set H := M  , the derived subgroup, so that |M : H| = 2,
                                                                                                                    and adopt the notation in Notation 3.3, with T = G. We argue as in the case of
                                                                                                                    T = ON in Proposition 4.12: we check, using GAP [35], that each of the 2-point
                                                                                                                    stabilizers M ∩ Mj in the T -action on [T : M ] satisﬁes (M ∩ Mj )H = M , that
                                                                                                                    is to say, condition (ii) of Theorem 3.10(1) holds. On the other hand, T [T :M] =
                                                                                                                    T (2),[T :M] by Lemma 4.3(b)(i) since T = Aut(T ) and T [T :M] is not 2-transitive.
                                                                                                                    Hence Theorem 3.10(1) applies, and we conclude that T [T :H] is not 2-closed. Hence,
                                                                                                                    T is not totally 2-closed.

                                                                                                                    Proposition 4.15. Fischer’s baby monster B is not totally 2-closed.

                                                                                                                    Proof. Let T = B, and consider the maximal subgroup M = 2.2 E6 (2).2. Then
                                                                                                                    M/Z(M ) is an extension of 2 E6 (2) by a graph automorphism. Let H = M  ∼             =
                                                                                                                      2                                               [T :M]
                                                                                                                    2. E6 (2), of index 2 in M . The stabilizers in T        of two distinct points are given
                                                                                                                    in [19, Lemma 2.25.1], namely
                                                                                                                              (2 × 21+20 .U6 (2)).2,   22 × F4 (2),   Fi22 : 2,   21+20 .U4 (3).22 .
                                                                                                                    We call these groups Ei = M ∩ Mi , for i = 2, 3, 4, 5, respectively. We claim that
                                                                                                                    HEi = M for i = 2, . . . , 5. All assertions in the next two paragraphs are from the
                                                                                                                    short proof of the main theorem in [25]. The groups Ei are the same as in [25], but
                                                                                                                    there the group M is denoted by E.

                                                                                                                        First, |M : E2 | is odd, so certainly E2 H = M . The group E3 contains Z(M ), and
                                                                                                                    E3 /Z(M ) is the centralizer in 2 E6 (2).2 of a graph automorphism. In particular, E3
                                                                                                                    contains a graph automorphism, so we also have E3 H = M . Next, M has precisely
                                                                                                                    two conjugacy classes of subgroups isomorphic to Fi22 : 2, and they are interchanged
                                                                                                                    by an automorphism of M which acts trivially on H (see [25, top of p. 1040]). It
                                                                                                                    follows, since E4 is one of these groups, that E4 ≤ H, and hence E4 H = M .

                                                                                                                    5. The Case T = J4
                   Bull. Math. Sci. 2024.14. Downloaded from www.worldscientific.com




                                                                                                                    In this section, we prove that the fourth Janko group J4 is totally 2-closed, and in
                                                                                                                    so-doing we prove Proposition 4.1 for J4 . This will complete the proofs of Theorem
                                                                                                                    1.1 and Proposition 4.1. Our main reference is Janko’s original paper [20], and
                                                                                                                    wherever possible we try to be consistent with his notation, or draw attention to

                                                                                                                         Throughout the section, we set T := J4 , and we adopt Strategy 4.5. To complete
                                                                                                                    Step 1 of Strategy 4.5, we need to know all maximal subgroups M of T such that

                                                                                                                    • D2 := CT (z) ∼ = 21+12 .3.M22 : 2. The subgroup O2 (D2 ) is not complemented in

                                                                                                                                                                                                 = L5 (2),
                                                                                                                      [20, Propositions 20 and 21].
                                                                                                                        Maximality of the subgroups D1 , D2 , and D3 can also be checked from the
                                                                                                                    Web Atlas [41]. For Strategy 4.5 we also need to examine transitive actions T [T :H]
                                                                                                                    with base size at least 3 for non-maximal subgroups H. For such a subgroup, if
                                                                                                                    H < M < T with M maximal, then T [T :M] also has base size at least 3, and hence
                                                                                                                    M is conjugate to Di for some i. In similar situations in Sec. 4, we determined
                                                                                                                    whether or not such an action T [T :H] has base size 2 by ﬁnding crude upper bounds
                                                                                                                    on |xT ∩ H| for each element x ∈ H of prime order, and then applying Proposition
                                                                                                                    4.2. For T = J4 , we need to be much more careful when ﬁnding upper bounds for
                                                                                                                    |xT ∩ H| in the case where x is an involution. Thus, the ﬁrst lemma in this section
                                                                                                                    counts involutions in subgroups of the maximal subgroups D1 , D2 , and D3 . Since

                                                                                                                                                          2350004-42
                                    March 13, 2024 14:46 WSPC/1664-3607                                                                                       319-BMS              2350004




                                                                                                                                                                                             Totally 2-closed groups


                                                                                                                    we make frequent reference to Janko’s paper [20], we summarize Janko’s notation
                                                                                                                    in Remark 5.1.

                                                                                                                    Remark 5.1. The Janko group T = J4 has precisely two classes of involutions,
                                                                                                                    denoted class 2A and 2B, and Janko uses z and f , respectively, to denote repre-
                                                                                                                    sentatives of these classes, [20, Theorem A(5)]. He also uses the following notation
                                                                                                                    for the subgroups D1 , D2 , and D3 :
by 137.205.72.35 on 02/10/26. Re-use and distribution is strictly not permitted, except for Open Access articles.




                                                                                                                    (1) Janko writes M = D1 , and K = F1 , so M = V K ∼           = 211 M24 with V ∩K = 1,
                                                                                                                        [20, Proposition 18].
                                                                                                                    (2) Janko writes H = D2 = CT (z), E = O2 (D2 ) ∼            = 21+12 , and H0 = [D2 , D2 ] ∼=
                                                                                                                          1+12
                                                                                                                        2       .3.M22 : 2 for the (index 2) derived subgroup of H, [20, Sec. 3]. In [20,
                                                                                                                        last 13 lines of Proposition 1], Janko describes the D2 -conjugacy classes of
                   Bull. Math. Sci. 2024.14. Downloaded from www.worldscientific.com




                                                                                                                        involutions in H0 : there are two classes in E\z, with representatives e and f ,
                                                                                                                        and four classes in H0 \E, with representatives t , t z, t1 , and t2 . Moreover all
                                                                                                                        of t , t z, t1 , t2 lie in the same coset of E, [20, p. 570, line-11]. As noted above,
                                                                                                                        f ∈ 2B; by [20, Proposition 9], the elements e, t , t1 all lie in class 2A, and
                                                                                                                        t z ∈ 2B; while by [20, Proposition 15], t2 ∈ 2B. Finally, by [20, Propositions
                                                                                                                        6 and 10], there are three D2 -conjugacy classes of involutions in H\H0 , with
                                                                                                                        representatives t1 , t1 z, and t2 , and by [20, Proposition 15], t1 ∈ 2A, and t1 z,
                                                                                                                        t2 ∈ 2B.
                                                                                                                    (3) Janko writes D3 = NT (A) = A  B, where A = 210 is self-centralizing with
                                                                                                                        A < D2 and B = F3 ∼             = L5 (2), [20, Propositions 20 and 21]. He notes that
                                                                                                                        O2 (D2 ) ∼  = 21+12 normalizes A = O2 (D3 ), and ND2 (A)/A is isomorphic to the
                                                                                                                        parabolic subgroup 26 : (Sym(3) × L3 (2)) of D3 /A ∼         =B ∼  = L5 (2), [20, p. 587,
                                                                                                                        lines 4–7].
                                                                                                                        To help us ﬁnd upper bounds for |xT ∩ H| in the case where x is an involution in
                                                                                                                    H < T , we introduce the following (non-standard) notation for counting involutions
                                                                                                                    in ﬁnite groups.

                                                                                                                    Notation 5.2. For a subset S of a ﬁnite group G, deﬁne
                                                                                                                                                       Inv(S : P1 , . . . , Pr )
                                                                                                                    to be the number of involutions in S with properties P1 , . . . , Pr . For example, if H
                                                                                                                    is a subgroup of Dj , for some j, then
                                                                                                                                              Inv(H\[Dj , Dj ] : 2-central in Dj )
                                                                                                                    is the number of involutions in H\[Dj , Dj ] which are centralized by a Sylow 2-
                                                                                                                    subgroup of Dj . We also deﬁne
                                                                                                                                     Inv(S) to be the total number of involutions in S,
                                                                                                                    and for S ⊆ J4 , we denote by Inv(S : 2A) and Inv(S : 2B) the number of involutions
                                                                                                                    in S in the conjugacy class 2A and 2B of J4 , respectively, so that
                                                                                                                                             Inv(S) = Inv(S : 2A) + Inv(S : 2B).

                                                                                                                                                              2350004-43
                                    March 13, 2024 14:46 WSPC/1664-3607                                                                                    319-BMS        2350004




                                                                                                                    M. Arezoomand et al.

                                                                                                                    in T = J4 . More precisely, we use the 112-dimensional representation for T over F2 .
                                                                                                                    The Magma code for this representation is available from the Web Atlas [41], and
                                                                                                                    it conveniently includes constructions of the subgroups D1 , D2 , D3 , and F3 deﬁned
                                                                                                                    above.

                                                                                                                       We now have the tools needed to prove Lemma 4.1 for J4 . Recall the notion of
                                                                                                                    the depth G (H) of a subgroup H of a group G introduced just before Strategy 4.5.

                                                                                                                       We are now ready to prove Proposition 6.1.

                                                                                                                    Proof of Proposition 6.1. By Proposition 6.3, we may assume that T is un-
                                                                                                                    twisted and that q = p is prime. Thus, by Propositions 2.12(a) and 6.4, we may
                                                                                                                    assume that T ∈ {F4 (p), E6 (p), E7 (p), E8 (p)}, and that p is an odd prime.
                                                                                                                         Let S be a maximally split torus in T , with (B, N ) a (B, N )-pair for T , with
                                                                                                                    respect to S. Then B has the form B = U  S, where U is a Sylow p-subgroup of
                                                                                                                    T . If T [T :B] is not 2-closed there is nothing further to prove for this group, so we
                                                                                                                    may assume that T [T :B] is 2-closed. Since p is odd, the group S has even order, and
                                                                                                                    hence has a subgroup R of index 2. Let H := U R. Then |B : H| = 2.
                                                                                                                         For the permutation group T [T :B] , the subgroup B is the stabilizer of the ‘point’
                                                                                                                    B. Each B-orbit in [T : B]\{B} is of the form {Bah | h ∈ B} for some a ∈ T \B.
                                                                                                                    Now, by Bruhat Normal Form [16, Theorem 2.3.5], we have T = BN B, so a = xny
                                                                                                                    for some x, y ∈ B and n ∈ N , and it follows that the B-orbit containing Ba also
                                                                                                                    contains Bay −1 = Bn, and the stabilizer in B of the point Bn is B ∩ B n . Since
                                                                                                                    N = NT (S), we have S ≤ B ∩ B n , and it follows that B = (B ∩ B n )H. This holds
                                                                                                                    for all n ∈ N .
                                                                                                                         Finally, by again using the fact that T = BN B, and arguing in exactly the
                                                                                                                    same way as in the ﬁnal paragraph of the proof of Proposition 6.4, we can see that
                                                                                                                    (B ∩ B t )H = B for all t ∈ T , and hence, after applying Theorem 3.10(1), that
                                                                                                                    T [T :H] is not 2-closed. Hence, T is not totally 2-closed.


                                                                                                                    6.1. Proof of Theorem 1.1
                                                                                                                    By Proposition 2.12, together with our results in Secs. 4–6, on sporadic simple
                                                                                                                    groups, and Proposition 6.1 in this section for the exceptional groups, we know
                                                                                                                    that each of the groups J1 , J3 , J4 , Th, Ly, M is totally 2-closed, and that these are
                                                                                                                    the only totally 2-closed simple groups. Thus Theorem 1.1 is proved.

                                                                                                                    7. Direct Products
                                                                                                                    In this section, our aim is to prove Theorem 1.2. For this reason, we assume through-
                                                                                                                    out the section that G is a nontrivial ﬁnite totally 2-closed group with F (G) = 1.
                                                                                                                    By Theorem 2.5, the group G must have the form G = T1 × · · · × Tr where for each
                                                                                                                    i ≤ r, Ti is a ﬁnite totally 2-closed nonabelian simple group, and Ti is not a section
                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                    of i=j Tj . Moreover, by Theorem 1.1, each of the Ti lies in the set
by 137.205.72.35 on 02/10/26. Re-use and distribution is strictly not permitted, except for Open Access articles.




                                                                                                                                                  S := {J1 , J3 , J4 , Th, Ly, M}.

                                                                                                                    By inspection of the sections of these sporadic simple groups, we see that there
                                                                                                                    exist distinct S, T ∈ S such that S is isomorphic to a section of T if and only if
                                                                                                                    S = Th and T = M, see Remark 2.6. Thus not both of the groups Th and M lie
                   Bull. Math. Sci. 2024.14. Downloaded from www.worldscientific.com




                                                                                                                    in {Ti : 1 ≤ i ≤ r}, and hence r ≤ 5 and one of the conditions (3)(i) or (3)(ii) of
                                                                                                                    Theorem 1.2 holds. This proves that each of the assertions (1)–(3) of Theorem 1.2
                                                                                                                    holds.
                                                                                                                                                                                                r
                                                                                                                        Thus to complete the proof of Theorem 1.2 we must show that, if G = i=1 Ti
                                                                                                                    with the Ti pairwise no-isomorphic, and if one of the conditions (3)(i) or (3)(ii) of
                                                                                                                    Theorem 1.2 holds, then G is totally 2-closed. Since none of the groups in S admits
                                                                                                                    a nontrivial factorization (Corollary 2.3), it follows from Proposition 2.10 that it
                                                                                                                    is suﬃcient to prove that ϕ(G) is 2-closed for each permutation representation
                                                                                                                    ϕ : G → Sym(Ω) (faithful and non-faithful) with |Ω| > 1 and ϕ(G) transitive. With
                                                                                                                    this in mind, we introduce the following hypothesis and notation, which we will
                                                                                                                    assume, for the remainder of the section.

                                                                                                                    Hypothesis 7.1. (a) The group G = T1 × · · · × Tr with the Ti pairwise non-
                                                                                                                      isomorphic, and either
                                                                                                                     (i) Ti ∈ {J1 , J3 , J4 , Th, Ly} for each i ≤ r; or
                                                                                                                    (ii) Ti ∈ {J1 , J3 , J4 , Ly, M} for each i ≤ r.

                                                                                                                    (b) We extend the notation for direct products introduced in Hypothesis 2.7.
                                                                                                                        Namely, for a direct product G1 × · · · × Gs of arbitrary ﬁnite groups Gi , and
                                                                                                                        each subgroup Li of Gi , we write

                                                                                                                              Li = {(x1 , . . . , xs ) : xi ∈ Li , and xj = 1 for j = i} ≤ G1 × · · · × Gs .

                                                                                                                    (c) Seeking a contradiction, we assume that G is not totally 2-closed, and that the
                                                                                                                        number r of simple direct summands is minimal with respect to this property.
                                                                                                                        Note that r > 1 by Theorem 1.1, and by Proposition 2.10, G has a proper
                                                                                                                        subgroup H such that G[G:H] is not 2-closed. Without loss of generality, we
                                                                                                                        may assume that the proper subgroup H is maximal by inclusion such that
                                                                                                                        G[G:H] is not 2-closed. By [39, Theorem 5.12 and Example 5.13], it follows that
                                                                                                                        H = 1. Further, H is core-free in G (since otherwise G/CoreG (H) ∼  = G[G:H] is
                                                                                                                        not totally 2-closed and is a direct product of less than r of the simple groups
                                                                                                                        in (i) or (ii), contradicting the minimality of r).

                                                                                                                                                              2350004-59
                                    March 13, 2024 14:46 WSPC/1664-3607                                                                                  319-BMS       2350004




                                                                                                                    M. Arezoomand et al.


                                                                                                                    (d) Next, write μi : G → Ti for the natural coordinate projection, for i ≤ r. Note
                                                                                                                        that μi (Ti ∩ H) is normal in μi (H), but to avoid cumbersome notation, we will
                                                                                                                        usually just say that Ti ∩ H is normal in μi (H).
                                                                                                                    (e) Our ﬁnal piece of notation is deﬁned with the minimality of r in mind: we set
                                                                                                                        G1 := T1 , and G2 := T2 × · · · × Tr , so that both G1 and G2 are ﬁnite totally
                                                                                                                        2-closed groups (by the minimality of r). We write the coordinate projections
                                                                                                                        here as π1 : G → G1 and π2 : G → G2 (so in particular π1 = μ1 ). We also set

                                                                                                                        Mi := πi (H) and Hi = G    i ∩ H, for i ∈ {1, 2}, where G i is as deﬁned in (b)
                                                                                                                        relative to the direct product G1 × G2 . Note that H is a subdirect subgroup
                                                                                                                        of M := M1 × M2 ≤ G and πi (Hi )  Mi for each i. As in part (d), we often
                                                                                                                        omit the πi , and just say that Hi  Mi . Since H is a subdirect subgroup of
                                                                                                                        M = M1 × M2 , it is important to note that M1 /H1 ∼       = M2 /H2 (Goursat’s
                   Bull. Math. Sci. 2024.14. Downloaded from www.worldscientific.com




                                                                                                                        Lemma, see [32, Theorem 4.8(i)]).

                                                                                                                    Remark 7.2. The ﬁnal piece of notation in Hypothesis 7.1 is introduced for con-
                                                                                                                    venience only: there will be nothing special about the labeling of the simple direct
                                                                                                                    factors of G, and we will sometimes vary the direct factor which is chosen to be T1
                                                                                                                    in our analysis. We warn the reader however, that the labeling of the direct factors
                                                                                                                    of G changes in this way, then the group M deﬁned in Hypothesis 7.1(e) may also
                                                                                                                    change.

                                                                                                                       In order to prove that each group G satisfying Hypothesis 7.1 is totally 2-closed,
                                                                                                                    we use the following strategy.

                                                                                                                    Strategy 7.3. Let G, Ti , H, etc. be as in Hypothesis 7.1. We follow the four steps
                                                                                                                    below.
                                                                                                                    Step 1: We prove (Lemma 7.4) that the subgroup M = M1 × M2 in Hypothesis
                                                                                                                    7.1(e) is a proper overgroup of H, that M is core-free in G, and that G[G:M] is
                                                                                                                    2-closed. This enables us to use the tools developed in Sec. 3, (see Notation 3.3).

                                                                                                                    Step 2: The tools developed in Sec. 3 also require information concerning the
                                                                                                                    transitive permutation group M [M:H] with point stabilizer H [M:H] . Note that H
                                                                                                                    is a subdirect subgroup of M = M1 × M2 . Step 2 comprises two results (Lem-
                                                                                                                    mas 7.5 and 7.6) concerning subdirect subgroups of a direct product of ﬁnite
                                                                                                                    groups.

                                                                                                                    Step 3: We prove (Lemma 7.7) that, for some i ≤ r, the permutation group
                                                                                                                     [T :μ (H)]
                                                                                                                    Ti i i       has base size greater than 2, and so, by Proposition 4.1, this pair
                                                                                                                    (Ti , μi (H)) lies in Table 1.
                                                                                                                    Step 4: For each pair (Ti , μi (H)) in Table 1, we examine the structure of X :=
                                                                                                                    G(2),[G:H] using Theorem 3.10(2), seeking a contradiction. We use the same notation
                                                                                                                    as that introduced in Notation 3.3 with some small changes given in Notation 7.9.

                                                                                                                       We begin with Step 1.

                                                                                                                    Lemma 7.4. Let G, r, Ti , H, M be as in Hypothesis 7.1. Then,
                                                                                                                     (i) μi (H) = Ti for any i ≤ r, M is core-free in G, G[G:M] is 2-closed, and H <
                                                                                                                         M < G; and
                                                                                                                    (ii) For each i ≤ r, and each composition factor S of μi (H)/(Ti ∩ H), there exists
                                                                                                                         j = i such that μj (H) has a composition factor isomorphic to S.

                                                                                                                    Proof. (i) Note that Hypothesis 2.7 also holds for G (with projection maps G → Ti
by 137.205.72.35 on 02/10/26. Re-use and distribution is strictly not permitted, except for Open Access articles.




                                                                                                                    now called μi ). Hence, since H is core-free in G by Hypothesis 7.1(c), it follows from
                                                                                                                    Lemma 2.8 that μi (H) = Ti for any i ≤ r. Then, since M ≤ μ1 (H) × · · · × μr (H),
                                                                                                                    the group M does not contain T̂i , for any i ≤ r, and so M is core-free in G. Also,
                                                                                                                    (see Hypothesis 7.1(e)), M = M1 × M2 < G1 × G2 , and by the minimality of r,
                                                                                                                     [G :M ]
                                                                                                                    Gi i i is 2-closed for i ∈ {1, 2}. Hence G[G:M] is 2-closed, by [10, Theorem 5.1].
                   Bull. Math. Sci. 2024.14. Downloaded from www.worldscientific.com




                                                                                                                    In particular, since by assumption G[G:H] is not 2-closed, we have H < M < G.
                                                                                                                    This proves part (i).
                                                                                                                       (ii) In order to prove part (ii) we will prove the following claim:
                                                                                                                    Claim: Let S be a ﬁnite simple group, and let X1 , . . . , Xt be ﬁnite groups (t ≥ 1)
                                                                                                                    such that no Xi has a section isomorphic to S. If X is a subdirect subgroup of
                                                                                                                    X1 × · · · × Xt , then X has no section isomorphic to S.
                                                                                                                        First, we see that part (ii) follows from the claim. Indeed, assume that the
                                                                                                                    claim holds, and that S is a composition factor of μi (H)/(Ti ∩ H), for some i ≤ r.
                                                                                                                    Without loss of generality assume that i = 1, so S is a composition factor of
                                                                                                                    μ1 (H)/(T1 ∩ H) = M1 /H1 . Since H is a subdirect subgroup of M = M1 × M2
                                                                                                                    (Hypothesis 7.1(e)), we have M1 /H1 ∼ = M2 /H2 , and hence S is a composition factor
                                                                                                                    of M2 . Then since M2 = π2 (H) is a subdirect subgroup of μ2 (H) × · · · × μr (H),
                                                                                                                    it follows from the claim that μj (H) has a composition factor isomorphic to S for
                                                                                                                    some j ≥ 2.
                                                                                                                    Proof of the Claim: The proof is by induction on t. The case t = 1 is trivially
                                                                                                                    true, so assume that t > 1 and that the claim holds for direct products of less than
                                                                                                                    t groups. Suppose that X is a subdirect subgroup of X1 × · · · × Xt , that no Xi has
                                                                                                                    a section isomorphic to S, but that X has a section isomorphic to S, say S ∼         = Y /N
                                                                                                                    with N  Y ≤ X. We will derive a contradiction. For each i ≤ r, let νi : X → Xi be
                                                                                                                    the natural projection map and Yi = νi (Y ), so Y is a subdirect subgroup of Z :=
                                                                                                                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                    Y1 ×· · ·×Yt and no Yi has a section isomorphic to S. Further let νi : Z → j=i Yj be
                                                                                                                    the natural projection map, for each i, and note that ν1 (Y ) is a subdirect subgroup
                                                                                                                    of Y2 × · · · × Yt . Hence, if ν1 (Y ) has a section isomorphic to S, then by induction Yi
                                                                                                                    has a section isomorphic to S, for some i ≥ 2, which is a contradiction. Hence ν1 (Y )
                                                                                                                    has no section isomorphic to S. Since ν1 (Y )/ν1 (N ) is isomorphic to a quotient of
                                                                                                                    the simple group Y /N ∼      = S, this implies that ν1 (N ) = ν1 (Y ). Now, the kernel of
                                                                                                                    ν1 |Y is the group K := Y ∩ Y1 , and so ν1 (N ) = ν1 (Y ) implies that Y = N K,
                                                                                                                      

                                                                                                                    whence K/(N ∩ K) ∼      = N K/N = Y /N ∼       = S. Thus, Y1 ∼
                                                                                                                                                                                  = Y1 has a section isomorphic
                                                                                                                    to S, which is a contradiction. This completes the inductive proof of the claim, and
                                                                                                                    hence completes the proof of the lemma.

                                                                                                                    Lemma 7.5. Let X1 , . . . , Xt be ﬁnite groups, and let X be a subdirect subgroup of
                                                                                                                    X1 × · · · × Xt . Then the following assertions hold :
                                                                                                                                       i ≤ X for some i ∈ {1, 2}, then X = X1 × X2 .
                                                                                                                     (i) If t = 2, and X
                                                                                                                    (ii) Let p be a prime, and suppose that each group Xi is a transitive permutation
by 137.205.72.35 on 02/10/26. Re-use and distribution is strictly not permitted, except for Open Access articles.




                                                                                                                         group of p-power degree. Then the Fitting subgroup F (X) is a (possibly trivial)
                                                                                                                         p-group.

                                                                                                                    Proof. (i) This follows immediately from [32, Lemma 4.7].
                                                                                                                        (ii) For each i ≤ t, assume that Xi is a transitive permutation group on a set
                   Bull. Math. Sci. 2024.14. Downloaded from www.worldscientific.com




                                                                                                                    Ωi with |Ωi | a power of p, and let νi : X → Xi be the natural projection map. It
                                                                                                                    is suﬃcient to show that νi (F (X)) is a p-group for each i. Note that, for each i,
                                                                                                                    νi (F (X)) is a nilpotent normal subgroup of νi (X) = Xi (since X is subdirect), and
                                                                                                                    hence νi (F (X)) ≤ F (Xi ). If νi (F (X)) = 1 there is nothing to prove so assume that
                                                                                                                    νi (F (X)) = 1 and let q be a prime dividing |νi (F (X))|. Then the unique (nontrivial)
                                                                                                                    Sylow q-subgroup Q of νi (F (X)) is characteristic in νi (F (X)) and hence normal in
                                                                                                                    Xi . Since Xi is transitive on Ωi , all the orbits of its normal subgroup Q have the
                                                                                                                    same size, say m. Thus m divides |Ωi | which is a power of p, and also m divides |Q|
                                                                                                                    which is a power of q. It follows that p = q, and hence that νi (F (X)) is a p-group.
                                                                                                                    Thus part (ii) is proved.

                                                                                                                    Lemma 7.6. Let E be a ﬁnite group, let θ ∈ Aut(E), and let
                                                                                                                                                   J := {(e, eθ ) : e ∈ E},
                                                                                                                    a full diagonal subgroup of X := E × E. Then:
                                                                                                                      (i) CoreX (J) = {(z, z θ ) : z ∈ Z(E)} = Z(X) ∩ J.
                                                                                                                     (ii) The group Y := X [X:J] is a central product E1 ◦ E2 , where Ei ∼
                                                                                                                                                                                         = E for each i,
                                                                                                                                      ∼
                                                                                                                          and E1 ∩ E2 = Z(E). In particular Y = X/(Z(X) ∩ J).
                                                                                                                    (iii) Writing U for the image of a subgroup U ≤ Y under the natural projection
                                                                                                                          map Y → Y /(E1 ∩ E2 ), we have Y ∼   = E1 × E2 , and J is a subdirect subgroup
                                                                                                                          such that
                                                                                                                                                      J ∩ E1 = J ∩ E2 = 1.

                                                                                                                    Proof. (i) and (ii): Since part (ii) follows immediately from (i), we only need to
                                                                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                    prove (i). Let x ∈ CoreX (J) = y∈X J y . Then x = (e, eθ ) for some e ∈ E (since
                                                                                                                    x ∈ J), and also xy ∈ J for all y = (e1 , e2 ) ∈ X. In particular, taking y = (1, e2 ),
                                                                                                                    we have xy = (e, eθe2 ) ∈ J, so eθe2 = eθ , and this holds for all e2 ∈ E. Hence
                                                                                                                    eθ ∈ Z(E), and since θ is an automorphism, it follows that e ∈ Z(E). Thus,
                                                                                                                    CoreX (J) ⊆ {(z, z θ ) : z ∈ Z(E)}. The reverse inclusion clearly holds, so equality
                                                                                                                    holds and hence part (i), and also part (ii), are proved.

                                                                                                                    subgroup of N := μ1 (H)× · · ·× μr (H) since M ≤ N (Hypothesis 7.1(e)). Since H is

                                                                                                                    (Ti , μi (H)) from Table 1. First, we deal with the unique pair in Table 1 involving
                                                                                                                    the Monster, namely, (M, 2.B).
                                                                                                                    Lemma 7.8. For Ti , μi , H as in Hypothesis 7.1, no pair (Ti , μi (H)) is equal to
                                                                                                                    (M, 2.B).

                                                                                                                    Proof. Suppose to the contrary that (Ti , μi (H)) = (M, 2.B), for some i. As dis-
                                                                                                                    cussed in Remark 7.2, we may assume that i = 1, so M1 = 2.B, and by Hypoth-
                                                                                                                    esis 7.1, Tj ∈ {J1 , J3 , J4 , Ly} for each j ≥ 2. Now, H is a subdirect subgroup of
                                                                                                                    M = M1 × M2 , and by Lemma 7.4(i), H is a proper subgroup of M . Thus, by
                                                                                                                    Lemma 7.5(i), H does not contain M1 , so H1 = T1 ∩ H = M1 ∩ H is a proper
                                                                                                                    normal subgroup of M1 = 2.B. It follows that B is a composition factor of M1 /H1 ,
                                                                                                                    but this contradicts Lemma 7.4(ii) since, for each j ≥ 2, Tj ∈ {J1 , J3 , J4 , Ly} and
                                                                                                                    none of these simple groups has a section isomorphic to B.

                                                                                                                    Remark 7.12. We make a preliminary remark about how we may exploit
                                                                                                                    Lemma 7.11(ii) in the proof of Theorem 1.2: suppose that, for a ﬁxed pair (T1 , M1 ),
                                                                                                                    we have used Lemmas 7.10 and 7.11 to show that a(G, M, H) is a power of a prime
                                                                                                                    p, and hence, by Lemma 7.11(ii) that F (X) is a p-group. Suppose that we then con-
by 137.205.72.35 on 02/10/26. Re-use and distribution is strictly not permitted, except for Open Access articles.




                                                                                                                    sider a pair (Tj , μj (H)) where 2 ≤ j ≤ r. By changing the labeling, we can replace
                                                                                                                    (T1 , M1 ) by (Tj , μj (H)), but in doing this we change the overgroup M of H, say
                                                                                                                    to M . It may be possible to use Lemmas 7.10 and 7.11 to show that a(G, M , H) is
                                                                                                                    a power of a prime s, with s = p, whence by Lemma 7.11(ii), F (X) is an s-group,
                                                                                                                    implying that F (X) = 1. This strategy proves to be very useful. We emphasize
                   Bull. Math. Sci. 2024.14. Downloaded from www.worldscientific.com




                                                                                                                    that, when we change the labeling, even though the subgroup M may change, the
                                                                                                                    group X = G(2),Ω and its subgroup H do not change.

                                                                                                                    8. Concluding Remarks: The General Case
                                                                                                                    As a result of the work in this paper, the task of classifying all ﬁnite totally 2-closed
                                                                                                                    groups G can now be reduced to the case where G is insoluble and F (G) > 1 (see
                                                                                                                    Question 1 in Sec. 1.1). We conclude the paper with some remarks about this case,

                                                                                                                                                            2350004-70
                                    March 13, 2024 14:46 WSPC/1664-3607                                                                                    319-BMS        2350004




                                                                                                                                                                                       Totally 2-closed groups


                                                                                                                    and a reduction theorem.
                                                                                                                        We note ﬁrst that a crucial step in our classiﬁcation was the essential reduction
                                                                                                                    to classifying those ﬁnite groups (with trivial Fitting subgroup) which are 2-closed in
                                                                                                                    all of their transitive permutation representations (see Proposition 2.10). Although
                                                                                                                    we weren’t able to reduce our study of arbitrary ﬁnite totally 2-closed groups to
                                                                                                                    transitive actions, the following theorem (and subsequent corollary) signiﬁcantly
                                                                                                                    reduces the types of faithful actions that need to be examined. In order to state it,
by 137.205.72.35 on 02/10/26. Re-use and distribution is strictly not permitted, except for Open Access articles.




                                                                                                                    we need some additional terminology: Permutation representations of a group G on
                                                                                                                    sets Γ and Γ are said to be permutationally equivalent if there exists a bijection
                                                                                                                    f : Γ → Γ such that, for all γ ∈ Γ and all g ∈ G, the image (γ g )f = (γf )g . Note
                                                                                                                    that f induces a bijection Γ × Γ → Γ × Γ , namely, f : (α, β) → (αf, βf ), and that
                                                                                                                    this induced map sends G-orbits in Γ × Γ to G-orbits in Γ × Γ .
                   Bull. Math. Sci. 2024.14. Downloaded from www.worldscientific.com




                                                                                                                        Our general reduction theorem can now be stated as follows.

                                                                                                                    Theorem 8.1. Let G ≤ Sym(Ω), and suppose that Γ, Γ are distinct G-orbits on
                                                                                                                    which the G-actions are permutationally equivalent relative to a bijection f : Γ → Γ .
                                                                                                                    Let Ω := Ω\Γ, so Ω = Ω ∪ Γ. Then

                                                                                                                    (a) both G and G(2),Ω act faithfully on Ω , and
                                                                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                    (b) The restriction G(2),Ω |Ω = G(2),Ω .
                                                                                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                    (c) If G is ﬁnite, then G = G(2),Ω if and only if GΩ = G(2),Ω .

                                                                                                                    Proof. (a) Note ﬁrst that since G(2),Ω has the same orbits as G in Ω, the set
                                                                                                                    Ω is G(2),Ω -invariant. Also, G ≤ G(2),Ω . To prove (a), it is therefore suﬃcient to
                                                                                                                    show that G(2),Ω is faithful on Ω . So assume that x ∈ G(2),Ω such that x ﬁxes Ω
                                                                                                                    pointwise, and let γ ∈ Γ. Then γf ∈ Γ ⊆ Ω , so (γf )x = γf . By Theorem 2.4,
                                                                                                                    there exists g ∈ G such that γ x = γ g and (γf )x = (γf )g . Thus γf = (γf )g , and by
                                                                                                                    the deﬁning property of f , (γf )g = (γ g )f . This implies that γf = (γ g )f = (γ x )f ,
                                                                                                                    and since f is a bijection we deduce that γ = γ x . It follows that x ﬁxes Γ pointwise,
                                                                                                                    and hence that x = 1. This proves part (a).
                                                                                                                         (b) Let g ∈ G(2),Ω . Then g leaves invariant each G-orbit in Ω × Ω. In particular,
                                                                                                                      Ω                                                                                 
                                                                                                                    g leaves invariant each G-orbit in Ω × Ω and hence (see [40, Remark 4.2]) g Ω ∈
                                                                                                                                                                                                         
                                                                                                                    G(2),Ω . Thus G(2),Ω |Ω ≤ G(2),Ω . To prove the reverse inclusion let x ∈ G(2),Ω .
                                                                                                                    We extend the deﬁnition of x to a permutation y ∈ Sym(Ω) by deﬁning γ y = γ x
                                                                                                                    if γ ∈ Ω , and γ y = ((γf )x )f −1 if γ ∈ Γ. Since f : Γ → Γ is a bijection, y is a
                                                                                                                    permutation of Ω.
                                                                                                                         We claim that y ∈ G(2),Ω . Note that this claim implies that each element of
                                                                                                                      (2),Ω
                                                                                                                    G        lies in G(2),Ω |Ω , and hence a proof of the claim completes the proof of part
                                                                                                                    (b). By deﬁnition, y leaves invariant all the G-orbits in Ω × Ω , so we need to
                                                                                                                    consider G-orbits Δ contained in Γ1 × Γ2 where the Γi are G-orbits in Ω and at
                                                                                                                    least one is equal to Γ.
                                                                                                                         Suppose ﬁrst that Γ1 = Γ2 = Γ and deﬁne Δ = {(αf, βf ) | (α, β) ∈ Δ}. To
                                                                                                                    see that Δ is G-invariant let g ∈ G and (αf, βf ) ∈ Δ . Then, using the deﬁning

                                                                                                                    ((αf )x f −1 , (βf )x f −1 ) and we have to prove that this lies in Δ. By the deﬁnition

                                                                                                                    f , (βf )g = (β g )f . Thus

                                                                                                                    since Δ is G-invariant. Thus y leaves Δ invariant in this case also. It follows that y
                                                                                                                    leaves invariant each G-orbit in Ω × Ω and hence y ∈ G(2),Ω . Part (b) follows.
